newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh hopes jute will survive competition.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh hopes jute will survive competition.

text.p: Jute still has a role in the world economy despite challenges from farmers switching to other crops and consumers turning to synthetics, jute producers said at a weekend meeting.
K.M. Rabbani, executive director of International Jute Organisation (IJO), said on Saturday that the low price of jute had been forcing farmers to switch to other crops.

"At the farmers' end, jute is facing competition of other crops which are becoming more remunerative than jute," Rabbani told a three-day meeting of the International Jute Council, the governing body of the IJO.
Despite challenges, Rabbani said, the fibre had a future.
"Jute is a renewable and bio-degradable natural resource grown easily in this part (tropical) of the world," he said.
Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria said while opening the conference he hoped the natural fibre would survive the threat from synthetics in the world market and regain its lost glory.
"The jute will survive as long as the sun and earth exist, but the synthetics will not because the minerals or hydrocarbons will exhaust one day," he said.
The Dhaka-based IJO groups five producing countries -- Bangladesh, India, China, Nepal and Thailand -- and 22 consuming nations, mostly in the West.
Kibria said jute was facing "serious competition" from synthetics and other substitutes in the world market.

"The problem has been compounded by the fact farmers are not getting remunerative prices for jute while operations of jute mills are not efficient because of old machines and a variety of other reasons related to labour and shortcomings," he said.

IJO officials said the livelihood of more than 10 million small and marginal farmers of jute-producing countries depended on the future of jute, which is mainly used for making sacks and carpet-backing cloths.

"The jute is an important cash crop for millions of poor farmers of many countries in the region, and as such, development of jute economy will have positive impact on poverty alleviation," said Kibria.
Bangladesh officials said the country's annual jute export earnings had dropped to about $250 million presently from nearly $500 million in 1970s.
Rabbani said world production of raw jute, extracted from a reed-like plant, dropped to 2.58 million tonnes in 1995/96 (July-June) from 3.4 million tonnes in 1991/92.
World exports of jute and jute products fell to 1.23 million tonnes in 1994/95 from 1.5 million tonnes in 1989/90, he said.
The vice-chairman of the Bangladesh Jute Association, Rezaul Karim, said Bangladesh was in a better position with higher exports of raw jute to countries like China, Pakistan and India.
He said raw jute exports in the first nine months of fiscal year 1996/97 (July-June) jumped almost 50 percent to more than $90 million compared with the same period of 1995/96.
But the daily Financial Express said in an editorial on Sunday that any turnaround was unlikely as long as the majorty of the jute companies remained in the public sector.
"The need for privatisation cannot, therefore, be over emphasised. The government needs to show total political commitment to privatisation in the jute industry," it said.
